title: Stratford-upon-Avon
subtitle: Shakespeare's life, walked in order
intro: Shakespeare's whole life, walked in order through the town where it happened: a family in trouble, a schoolboy, a marriage at 18, a rise in London, a servant of the king, and a legend.

dayGlance.title: His youth
dayGlance.sub: The Birthplace, his school and Anne Hathaway's Cottage.

dayGlance.title: The legend
dayGlance.sub: The theatre, the statue and the river.

actsLede: Six parts, in the order he lived them.

acts.label: Act 1 · 1564: born into trouble
acts.tagline: A family that climbed, then fell.
acts.narrative: His father married into a landowning family, rose to run the town, then was taken to court and fell into debt.

acts.label: Act 2 · The schoolboy
acts.tagline: A free school, and the first actors in town.
acts.narrative: Latin six days a week, and the first touring actors performing in the hall downstairs.

acts.label: Act 3 · Married at 18
acts.tagline: A wife, three children, then gone.
acts.narrative: He married an older, pregnant farmer's daughter, had three children by 20, and left for London.

acts.label: Act 4 · The rise
acts.tagline: From a nobody to an owner.
acts.narrative: Mocked as an upstart, he wrote for a rich patron in the plague years, then became an owner of his company and of the Globe.

acts.label: Act 5 · The king's man, and the end
acts.tagline: Royal servant, rich man, a grave he paid for.
acts.narrative: The king took over his company. He invested at home, protected his daughter in his will, and paid for his own grave.

acts.label: Act 6 · The legend
acts.tagline: The family ended. The name didn't.
acts.narrative: His friends saved his plays, a rained-out festival made Stratford famous, and his birthplace was nearly shipped to America.

The Birthplace has timed entry, so book ahead. To do it all in one day, start at the Birthplace at 10: New Place has the shortest hours (11 to 3 in autumn), and the church is only open on Sunday afternoons. Hall's Croft and Mary Arden's Farm are closed to visitors. Coming twice instead? Split after Anne Hathaway's Cottage: his youth on the first visit, then the rise, the end and the legend on the second.

planCard.todo: Park at Bridgeway, then walk to Henley Street along Bridge Street.

birthplace.name: Shakespeare's Birthplace
birthplace.onCamera: This is where it all starts. William Shakespeare was born in this house in 1564. Today he's probably the most famous writer in the world. But he didn't start out important. His family was ordinary. And when he was a boy, they got into serious trouble. I think that explains everything he did later.
facts: The first record of his family is right here. In 1552, his father was fined for leaving a pile of rubbish and dung in this street.

His father, John, made gloves. His mother, Mary Arden, came from a farming family that owned its own land. In fact, John's father rented his farm from Mary's father. John kept moving up. He bought houses, joined the town council, and in 1568 he became head of the town, like a mayor.

Then it all went wrong. He was taken to court for selling wool without permission, and for charging too much interest on loans. He got into debt and stopped going to council meetings. He asked for a family badge, called a coat of arms, but he didn't get it. William was about 12.
birthplace.closeOnCamera: So that's the boy. His family climbed up, then fell. Everything he did later, the money, the houses, the family badge, was about climbing back. And it started at school, five minutes down the road.

routeCard.note: Enter through the Shakespeare Centre on Henley Street.

see: The room where he was born
The old timber fronts of Henley Street
planCard.todo: Timed entry, so book ahead. Open 10 to 5 from spring to autumn. Your ticket also covers New Place. Then walk to the school, about 6 minutes.

schoolroom.name: Shakespeare's Schoolroom and Guildhall
schoolroom.onCamera: This is almost certainly where Shakespeare went to school. Think about that. The boy who wrote Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet and Macbeth had his lessons in this room. And the hall downstairs is part of his story too.
facts: It was a free school for boys from the town. Lessons were in Latin, from early morning to late afternoon, Monday to Saturday. Nobody can prove he came here. But it was free, it was five minutes from his house, and his father was one of the town's leaders.

In 1568, travelling actors came to Stratford for the first time on record. They performed in the hall downstairs. That year his father was head of the town, so he would have been watching. William was four.
schoolroom.closeOnCamera: He never went to university. That's why some people still say a lord must have written his plays. Remember that, because in London, people will laugh at him for it. But first, at 18, he married a farmer's daughter from Shottery, a village a mile away. Let's walk there.

routeCard.note: The schoolroom is upstairs. The Guildhall, the medieval town hall, is downstairs.

see: On the way: Harvard House on High Street (1596), the family home of John Harvard's mother. Harvard University is named after him.
Timber houses from the 1400s next door, built for poor old people
planCard.todo: Open 11 to 5, last entry 4:15. £10 if you add it to your Birthplace ticket, £15 on its own. Then walk to Anne Hathaway's Cottage in Shottery, about 25 minutes.

anne-hathaway.name: Anne Hathaway's Cottage
anne-hathaway.onCamera: This is where Anne Hathaway grew up. In 1582, William Shakespeare married her. He was 18. She was 26, and she was already pregnant. It was one of the biggest decisions of his life, and it shaped everything that came next.
facts: In Shakespeare's time, this was Hewlands Farm, with more than 90 acres. Anne's family farmed here for generations. Her father had died the year before the wedding.
Their daughter Susanna was born six months after the wedding. Two years later, they had twins, Hamnet and Judith. By 20, William had a wife and three children.
anne-hathaway.closeOnCamera: Then, at some point, he left. Anne and the children stayed in Stratford, and William went to London. For about seven years after the twins were born, nobody knows where he was. Historians call them the lost years. When we find him again, he's in London, and he's about to get rich.

routeCard.sub: Cottage Lane, Shottery · a mile from the centre
routeCard.note: About 25 minutes on foot from the school.

planCard.todo: Open 10 to 5. £5 if you add it to your Birthplace ticket. Then walk back into the centre to New Place, about 25 minutes.

new-place.name: Shakespeare's New Place
new-place.onCamera: This is where Shakespeare lived when he was rich. He bought a house on this spot in 1597, when he was 33. It was one of the biggest houses in his home town. Five years before that, people in London were laughing at him. So how did a glove-maker's son do it? Here's how.
facts: The first time he's mentioned in London, it's an insult. In 1592, a jealous writer called him an 'upstart crow'. He meant: a nobody. An actor with no university education, who thought he could write as well as them.
Then a plague closed London's theatres for more than a year. So he wrote poems for a rich young lord. One of them became the biggest bestseller of his life.

When the theatres opened again in 1594, he made the smartest move of his life. He didn't just write for an acting company. He became one of its owners. They performed for Queen Elizabeth the First. And now he got a share of all the money, not just pay for his writing.

In 1598, the man who owned the land under their theatre wanted them out. So while he was away for Christmas, the company took the whole theatre apart. They carried the wood across the river, and used it to build the Globe. Shakespeare owned part of it.
new-place.closeOnCamera: And he brought the money home. In 1596, he finally got his father the family badge. Now they were officially upper class. But that same year, his only son, Hamnet, died. He was 11. A year later, Shakespeare bought the house that stood right here. So where is it? In 1759, it belonged to a priest. Tourists kept coming, and he argued with the town about tax. So he knocked it down.

routeCard.note: Enter by the gate on Chapel Street.

see: The garden where the house stood
Nash's House next door: the home of Thomas Nash, who married Shakespeare's granddaughter Elizabeth
planCard.todo: Included in your Birthplace ticket. Check the hours: in autumn it's open 11 to 3. Then walk to Holy Trinity, about 7 minutes.

holy-trinity.name: Holy Trinity Church
holy-trinity.angle: 1603–1616 · The king's man, and the end
holy-trinity.onCamera: By the end of his life, Shakespeare was more than a writer. He worked for the king. He owned land and houses. He was one of the richest men in his home town. He came back to Stratford for his last years, and he died in 1616, at 52. This is his grave. And he even paid for this spot.
facts: In 1603, the new king, James the First, made Shakespeare's company his own. They became the King's Men. Shakespeare's name was second on the list. He was even given red cloth for a royal uniform.

He kept spending his money at home. In 1605, he paid £440, a huge amount then, for a share of the money the church collected. That gave him the right to be buried inside, next to the altar. Most people were buried outside.

A month before he died, he changed his will. His daughter Judith had just married a man who was caught in a scandal. So Shakespeare made sure that man couldn't take her money. And his wife, Anne? He left her only one thing by name: his 'second-best bed'.
holy-trinity.closeOnCamera: Look at the stone. It says: 'Cursed be he that moves my bones.' In other words: don't touch my bones. In 2016, scientists scanned the grave. It looks like someone dug near his head. There's an old story that his skull was stolen. The church doesn't believe it. And here's the sad part. He spent his life building a family name. But his last grandchild died in 1670, with no children. The family ended. The name didn't.

routeCard.note: Go in by the avenue of lime trees.

see: On the way: Hall's Croft, where his daughter Susanna lived with her husband, Dr John Hall. They married in this church in 1607.
planCard.todo: Hours change with the day and the season, and on Sundays it's only open in the afternoon. The grave costs £5. It's a working church, so keep your voice down. Then walk along the river to the theatre, about 8 minutes.

theatre.name: The Royal Shakespeare Theatre
theatre.angle: After 1616 · How he became a legend
theatre.onCamera: When Shakespeare died, he was famous in London. But he wasn't a legend yet. That took a book, a party that went badly wrong, and a rumour about an American showman. And a lot of it happened right here.
facts: Seven years after he died, two actors from his company printed his plays in one big book, the First Folio. Eighteen of the plays had never been printed before, including Macbeth and The Tempest. Without that book, we'd probably have lost them.

In 1769, the most famous actor in Britain at the time, David Garrick, held a three-day party here for Shakespeare. It rained non-stop. The river rose. And not one Shakespeare play was performed. But it worked. After that, people started coming to Stratford to see where he lived.

In 1847, the house where he was born went up for sale. Newspapers said an American showman, P. T. Barnum, wanted to buy it and ship it to America. He probably never really tried. But people panicked. The writer Charles Dickens helped raise £3,000, and the house was saved.
theatre.closeOnCamera: This theatre opened in 1932, on the day Stratford celebrates his birthday. It was designed by a 29-year-old woman, Elisabeth Scott. Seventy architects entered the competition, and she was the only woman. Now, one last stop: his statue.

planCard.todo: Then walk on to the statue in Bancroft Gardens, about 3 minutes.

river.name: The statue, the garden and the bridge
river.onCamera: Shakespeare died 400 years ago. But you've probably used his words without knowing it. He changed the way we talk, and the way England sees its own history. This whole town still lives off his name. So what did he leave behind?
facts: 'Green-eyed monster.' 'A wild-goose chase.' 'It's all Greek to me.' We still say these today, and they come from his plays. People say he invented 1,700 words. That's too many. But hundreds of words and phrases reached us through him.

He also changed how England sees its past. In his play, King Richard the Third is a famous villain. But Shakespeare was writing for Queen Elizabeth the First, and it was her grandfather who took Richard's crown. In 1944, during the Second World War, the British government paid for a film of his play Henry the Fifth. It's about an English king who invades France and wins. It came out the same year as D-Day, to lift people's spirits.
river.closeOnCamera: He was a glove-maker's son from a small country town. In London, they laughed at him. Then he got rich, and he worked for the king. And 400 years later, we have this theatre, this statue, and the words we still speak.

The narrowboats in the canal basin

coldOpen.title: Cold open
facts: Everyone knows this man as a poet. But there's another story about him, and I want to tell it. Today I'm walking through his whole life, in order, in the town where it happened. A family that lost everything. A young man everyone laughed at. A theatre taken apart in secret. And a grave with a curse on it.

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: So that's his life, from the house where he was born to this statue by the river. A family that fell. A schoolboy. A husband at 18. A man who got rich by owning, not just writing. A servant of the king. And a grave he paid for. His family ended, but his words didn't. If you enjoyed this, please like and subscribe, and tell me where I should go next.
